e-622.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity Vector Given the Acceleration Vector
e-622.problem:
The acceleration $\mathbf{a}$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
\mathbf{a}(t) = \langle 10, 0\rangle.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $\mathbf{v} = \langle 10,20\rangle$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
e-622.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨10,0⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 10\,\text{d}t,\int 0\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨10t+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{v} (1)= \langle 10,20\rangle.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨10(1)+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨10,20⟩ & =⟨10+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =10+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
C_2 = 20.
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨10t,\,20⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

e-623.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector at a Point in Time Given the Acceleration Vector
e-623.problem:
The acceleration $\mathbf{a}$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
\mathbf{a}(t) = \langle 2e^{2t}, 3e^{3t}\rangle.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $\mathbf{v} = \langle e^2, 2e^3 \rangle$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=2.$
e-623.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2{e}^{2t},3{e}^{3t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 3{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{2t}+{C}_{1},\,{e}^{3t}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{v}(1) = \langle e^2, 2e^3 \rangle.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨{e}^{2(1)}+{C}_{1},\,{e}^{3(1)}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{2},2{e}^{3}⟩ & =⟨{e}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,{e}^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have $C_1=0$ and $C_2 = e^3.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨{e}^{2t},\,{e}^{3t}+{e}^{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨{e}^{2(2)},\,{e}^{3(2)}+{e}^{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{4},\,{e}^{6}+{e}^{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

e-624.knowledge_point: Finding the Points at Which a Particle is Stationary Given the Acceleration Vector
e-624.problem:
The acceleration $\mathbf{a}$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
\mathbf{a}(t) = \langle 1, 2t \rangle, \quad -\infty <        t <        \infty.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $\mathbf{v} = \langle 2,0 \rangle$ when $t=1,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
e-624.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨1,2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 1\,\text{d}t,\int 2t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{v} (1)= \langle 2,0\rangle.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨1+{C}_{1},\,{1}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨2,0⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},\,1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have $C_1=1$ and $C_2=-1.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨t+1,\,{t}^{2}-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨t+1,\,{t}^{2}-1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}t+1 & =0\,⇒\,t=-1, \\ {t}^{2}-1=(t+1)(t-1) & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t= -1,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨3\sqrt{t},\,-\frac{4}{\sqrt{t+1}}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨2,\,-1⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the components of the the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$

$v(t)=⟨${{field-1}},{{field-2}}$⟩$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3\sqrt{t},\,-\frac{4}{\sqrt{t+1}}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 3\sqrt{t}\,\text{d}t,\int -\frac{4}{\sqrt{t+1}}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\sqrt{t}+{C}_{1},-8\sqrt{t+1}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨2,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨2\cdot 0\cdot \sqrt{0}+{C}_{1},-8\sqrt{0+1}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨2,-1⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},-8+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & ={C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =-8+{C}_{2} \\ {C}_{2} & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v(t)=⟨2t\sqrt{t}+2,\,-8\sqrt{t+1}+7⟩.
$$

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨3t,−4t+1⟩dt=⟨∫3tdt,∫−4t+1dt⟩=⟨2tt+C1,−8t+1+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(0)=⟨2,−1⟩. Substituting t=0, we get v(0)=⟨2⋅0⋅0+C1,−80+1+C2⟩⟨2,−1⟩=⟨C1,−8+C2⟩.

So, we must have 2=C1C1=2, and −1=−8+C2C2=7.

Therefore, the velocity vector is v(t)=⟨2tt+2,−8t+1+7⟩.

Question 2
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a=⟨1,2⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨4,3⟩ when t=1, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t.

a
v=⟨t+3,2t+1⟩
b
v=⟨t+4,2t+3⟩
c
v=⟨3t+1,4t+2⟩
d
v=⟨2t+4,4t+2⟩
e
v=⟨4t+3,3t+1⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating the acceleration gives v(t)=⟨t+C₁,2t+C₂⟩. Since v(1)=⟨4,3⟩, C₁=3 and C₂=1. Thus option a satisfies both the acceleration and initial velocity.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a=⟨1,2⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨4,3⟩$ when $t=1$, calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨1,2⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 1\,\text{d}t,\int 2\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t+{C}_{1},2t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨4,3⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨1+{C}_{1},2(1)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨4,3⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},2+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =1+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =3,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =2+{C}_{2} \\ {C}_{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v=⟨t+3,2t+1⟩.
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity Vector Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a=⟨1,2⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨4,3⟩$ when $t=1$, calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨1,2⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 1\,\text{d}t,\int 2\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t+{C}_{1},2t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨4,3⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨1+{C}_{1},2(1)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨4,3⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},2+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =1+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =3,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =2+{C}_{2} \\ {C}_{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v=⟨t+3,2t+1⟩.
$$

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨1t+1,4⟩,t∈[0,∞). Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨ln⁡10,3⟩ when t=1, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t.

a
v=⟨ln⁡(5t+5),2t+1⟩
b
v=⟨ln⁡(2t+8),t+2⟩
c
v=⟨ln⁡(5t+5),4t−1⟩
d
v=⟨ln⁡(t+1)ln⁡10ln⁡2,4t−1⟩
e
v=⟨ln⁡(t+1)ln⁡10ln⁡2,2t+1⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=⟨ln(t+1)+C₁,4t+C₂⟩. At t=1, C₁=ln(10)−ln(2)=ln(5) and C₂=−1. Since ln(t+1)+ln(5)=ln(5t+5), option c is correct.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨\frac{1}{t+1},4⟩,\,t\in [0,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡10,3⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{t+1},4⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{t+1}\,\text{d}t,\int 4\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+{C}_{1},4t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡10,3⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+1)+{C}_{1},4(1)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡10,3⟩ & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2+{C}_{1},4+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡10 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡10-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ {C}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{10}{2}) \\ {C}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡5,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =4+{C}_{2} \\ {C}_{2} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+\operatorname{ln}⁡5,4t-1⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡[5(t+1)],4t-1⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(5t+5),4t-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨1t+1,4⟩,t∈[0,∞). Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨ln⁡10,3⟩ when t=1, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t.

a
v=⟨ln⁡(5t+5),2t+1⟩
b
v=⟨ln⁡(2t+8),t+2⟩
c
v=⟨ln⁡(5t+5),4t−1⟩
d
v=⟨ln⁡(t+1)ln⁡10ln⁡2,4t−1⟩
e
v=⟨ln⁡(t+1)ln⁡10ln⁡2,2t+1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨1t+1,4⟩dt=⟨∫1t+1dt,∫4dt⟩=⟨ln⁡(t+1)+C1,4t+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(1)=⟨ln⁡10,3⟩. Substituting t=1, we get v(1)=⟨ln⁡(1+1)+C1,4(1)+C2⟩⟨ln⁡10,3⟩=⟨ln⁡2+C1,4+C2⟩.

So, we must have ln⁡10=ln⁡2+C1C1=ln⁡10−ln⁡2C1=ln⁡(102)C1=ln⁡5, and 3=4+C2C2=−1.

Therefore, the velocity vector is v=⟨ln⁡(t+1)+ln⁡5,4t−1⟩=⟨ln⁡[5(t+1)],4t−1⟩=⟨ln⁡(5t+5),4t−1⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity Vector Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨\frac{1}{t+1},4⟩,\,t\in [0,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡10,3⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{t+1},4⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{t+1}\,\text{d}t,\int 4\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+{C}_{1},4t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡10,3⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+1)+{C}_{1},4(1)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡10,3⟩ & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2+{C}_{1},4+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡10 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡10-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ {C}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{10}{2}) \\ {C}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡5,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =4+{C}_{2} \\ {C}_{2} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+\operatorname{ln}⁡5,4t-1⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡[5(t+1)],4t-1⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(5t+5),4t-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have ln⁡10=ln⁡2+C1C1=ln⁡10−ln⁡2C1=ln⁡(102)C1=ln⁡5, and 3=4+C2C2=−1.

Therefore, the velocity vector is v=⟨ln⁡(t+1)+ln⁡5,4t−1⟩=⟨ln⁡[5(t+1)],4t−1⟩=⟨ln⁡(5t+5),4t−1⟩.

before.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨{e}^{2t},{e}^{3t}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨{e}^{2},{e}^{3}⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$

before.html:
Question 4
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨e2t,e3t⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨e2,e3⟩ when t=1, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t.

a
v=⟨12e2t−32e2,13e3t+23e3⟩
b
v=⟨32e2t+32e2,13e3t+23e3⟩
c
v=⟨12e2t−12e2,13e3t−23e3⟩
d
v=⟨12e2t+12e2,13e3t+23e3⟩
e
v=⟨12e2t+32e2,23e3t+23e3⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=⟨e^(2t)/2+C₁,e^(3t)/3+C₂⟩. The condition v(1)=⟨e²,e³⟩ gives C₁=e²/2 and C₂=2e³/3, so option d is correct.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨{e}^{2t},{e}^{3t}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨{e}^{2},{e}^{3}⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨{e}^{2t},{e}^{3t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t,\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+{C}_{1},\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}+{C}_{2}⟩\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨{e}^{2},{e}^{3}⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2(1)}+{C}_{1},\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3(1)}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{2},{e}^{3}⟩ & =⟨\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+{C}_{1},\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{3} & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3}+{C}_{2} \\ {C}_{2} & =\frac{2}{3}{e}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v=⟨\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2},\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}+\frac{2}{3}{e}^{3}⟩\,.
$$

Question 4
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨e2t,e3t⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨e2,e3⟩ when t=1, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t.

a
v=⟨12e2t−32e2,13e3t+23e3⟩
b
v=⟨32e2t+32e2,13e3t+23e3⟩
c

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity Vector Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨{e}^{2t},{e}^{3t}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨{e}^{2},{e}^{3}⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨{e}^{2t},{e}^{3t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t,\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+{C}_{1},\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}+{C}_{2}⟩\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨{e}^{2},{e}^{3}⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2(1)}+{C}_{1},\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3(1)}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{2},{e}^{3}⟩ & =⟨\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+{C}_{1},\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{3} & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3}+{C}_{2} \\ {C}_{2} & =\frac{2}{3}{e}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v=⟨\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2},\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}+\frac{2}{3}{e}^{3}⟩\,.
$$

Question 6

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨8t3,−1⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨−1,3⟩ when t=1, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t=3.

a
v(3)=⟨−3,4⟩
b
v(3)=⟨159,1⟩
c
v(3)=⟨6,−3⟩
d
v(3)=⟨162,1⟩
e
v(3)=⟨162,−3⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=⟨2t⁴+C₁,−t+C₂⟩. Using v(1)=⟨−1,3⟩ yields C₁=−3 and C₂=4. Thus v(3)=⟨162−3,−3+4⟩=⟨159,1⟩.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨8{t}^{3},-1⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨-1,\,3⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=3.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨8{t}^{3},-1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 8{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t,\,\int -1\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{4}+{C}_{1},\,-t+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨-1,3⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨2(1)^{4}+{C}_{1},\,-(1)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,3⟩ & =⟨2+{C}_{1},\,-1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-3$ and ${C}_{2}=4.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨2{t}^{4}-3,\,-t+4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=3$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨2(3)^{4}-3,\,-(3)+4⟩ \\  & =⟨159,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector at a Point in Time Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨8{t}^{3},-1⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨-1,\,3⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=3.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨8{t}^{3},-1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 8{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t,\,\int -1\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{4}+{C}_{1},\,-t+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨-1,3⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨2(1)^{4}+{C}_{1},\,-(1)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,3⟩ & =⟨2+{C}_{1},\,-1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-3$ and ${C}_{2}=4.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨2{t}^{4}-3,\,-t+4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=3$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨2(3)^{4}-3,\,-(3)+4⟩ \\  & =⟨159,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-1,1-t⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨0,1⟩$ when $t=3,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=0.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨{t}^{2}-1,1-t⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int ({t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t,\int (1-t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t+{C}_{1},t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(3)=⟨0,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}-3+{C}_{1},3-\frac{{3}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,1⟩ & =⟨6+{C}_{1},-\frac{3}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-6$ and ${C}_{2}=\frac{5}{2}.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t-6,t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{5}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}-0-6,0-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}+\frac{5}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-6,\frac{5}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨t2−1,1−t⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨0,1⟩ when t=3, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t=0.

a
v(0)=⟨−6,52⟩
b
v(0)=⟨1,−2⟩
c
v(0)=⟨−6,12⟩
d
v(0)=⟨4,−2⟩
e
v(0)=⟨4,52⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨t2−1,1−t⟩dt=⟨∫(t2−1)dt,∫(1−t)dt⟩=⟨t33−t+C1,t−t22+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(3)=⟨0,1⟩. Substituting t=3, we get v(3)=⟨333−3+C1,3−322+C2⟩⟨0,1⟩=⟨6+C1,−32+C2⟩, so we must have C1=−6 and C2=52. Therefore, the velocity is given by v(t)=⟨t33−t−6,t−t22+52⟩.

Finally, the velocity at time t=0 is v(0)=⟨033−0−6,0−022+52⟩=⟨−6,52⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector at a Point in Time Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-1,1-t⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨0,1⟩$ when $t=3,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=0.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨{t}^{2}-1,1-t⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int ({t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t,\int (1-t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t+{C}_{1},t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(3)=⟨0,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}-3+{C}_{1},3-\frac{{3}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,1⟩ & =⟨6+{C}_{1},-\frac{3}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-6$ and ${C}_{2}=\frac{5}{2}.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t-6,t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{5}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}-0-6,0-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}+\frac{5}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-6,\frac{5}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨12(1+2t)3,9(1−3t)2⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨1,6⟩ when t=0, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t=1.

a
v(1)=⟨−66,21⟩
b
v(1)=⟨85,−8⟩
c
v(1)=⟨112,10⟩
d
v(1)=⟨32,−49⟩
e
v(1)=⟨121,15⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=⟨(3/2)(1+2t)⁴+C₁,−(1−3t)³+C₂⟩. Using v(0)=⟨1,6⟩ gives C₁=−1/2 and C₂=7. Thus v(1)=⟨(3/2)81−1/2,8+7⟩=⟨121,15⟩.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨12(1+2t)^{3},9(1-3t)^{2}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨1,6⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=1.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨12(1+2t)^{3},9(1-3t)^{2}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 12(1+2t)^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int 9(1-3t)^{2}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(1+2t)^{4}+{C}_{1},\,-(1-3t)^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨1,6⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(1+2(0))^{4}+{C}_{1},\,-(1-3(0))^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,6⟩ & =⟨\frac{3}{2}+{C}_{1},\,-1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}$ and ${C}_{2}=7.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(1+2t)^{4}-\frac{1}{2},\,-(1-3t)^{3}+7⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(1+2(1))^{4}-\frac{1}{2},\,-(1-3(1))^{3}+7⟩ \\  & =⟨121,15⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}},t⟩,\,t\in (0,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨1,-1⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=4.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}},t⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\,\text{d}t,\int t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}+{C}_{1},\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{1}}+{C}_{1},\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,-1⟩ & =⟨-2+{C}_{1},\frac{1}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=3$ and ${C}_{2}=-\frac{3}{2}.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}+3,\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-\frac{3}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=4$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(4) & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{4}}+3,\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{3}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{13}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨1t3,t⟩,t∈(0,∞). Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨1,−1⟩ when t=1, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t=4.

a
v(4)=⟨1,72⟩
b
v(4)=⟨2,92⟩
c
v(4)=⟨2,132⟩
d
v(4)=⟨4,152⟩
e
v(4)=⟨4,132⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨1t3,t⟩dt=⟨∫1t3dt,∫tdt⟩=⟨−2t+C1,t22+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(1)=⟨1,−1⟩. Substituting t=1, we get v(1)=⟨−21+C1,122+C2⟩⟨1,−1⟩=⟨−2+C1,12+C2⟩, so we must have C1=3 and C2=−32. Therefore, the velocity is given by v(t)=⟨−2t+3,t22−32⟩.

Finally, the velocity at time t=4 is v(4)=⟨−24+3,422−32⟩=⟨2,132⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector at a Point in Time Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}},t⟩,\,t\in (0,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨1,-1⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=4.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}},t⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\,\text{d}t,\int t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}+{C}_{1},\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{1}}+{C}_{1},\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,-1⟩ & =⟨-2+{C}_{1},\frac{1}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=3$ and ${C}_{2}=-\frac{3}{2}.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}+3,\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-\frac{3}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=4$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(4) & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{4}}+3,\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{3}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{13}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨1−et/2,3⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨0,1⟩ when t=2, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t=0.

a
v(0)=⟨e−4e,1⟩
b
v(0)=⟨2e−4,1⟩
c
v(0)=⟨e−1,−5⟩
d
v(0)=⟨e−4e,−3⟩
e
v(0)=⟨2e−4,−5⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=⟨t−2e^(t/2)+C₁,3t+C₂⟩. Using v(2)=⟨0,1⟩ gives C₁=2e−2 and C₂=−5. Therefore v(0)=⟨2e−4,−5⟩.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨1-{e}^{t/2},3⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨0,1⟩$ when $t=2,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=0.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨1-{e}^{t/2},3⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (1-{e}^{t/2})\,\text{d}t,\int 3\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t-2{e}^{t/2}+{C}_{1},3t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(2)=⟨0,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨2-2{e}^{2/2}+{C}_{1},3(2)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,1⟩ & =⟨2-2e+{C}_{1},6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=2e-2$ and ${C}_{2}=-5.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨t-2{e}^{t/2}+2e-2,3t-5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨0-2{e}^{0/2}+2e-2,3(0)-5⟩ \\  & =⟨2e-4,-5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨1−et/2,3⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨0,1⟩ when t=2, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t=0.

a
v(0)=⟨e−4e,1⟩
b
v(0)=⟨2e−4,1⟩
c
v(0)=⟨e−1,−5⟩
d
v(0)=⟨e−4e,−3⟩
e
v(0)=⟨2e−4,−5⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨1−et/2,3⟩dt=⟨∫(1−et/2)dt,∫3dt⟩=⟨t−2et/2+C1,3t+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(2)=⟨0,1⟩. Substituting t=2, we get v(2)=⟨2−2e2/2+C1,3(2)+C2⟩⟨0,1⟩=⟨2−2e+C1,6+C2⟩, so we must have C1=2e−2 and C2=−5. Therefore, the velocity is given by v(t)=⟨t−2et/2+2e−2,3t−5⟩.

Finally, the velocity at time t=0 is v(0)=⟨0−2e0/2+2e−2,3(0)−5⟩=⟨2e−4,−5⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector at a Point in Time Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨1-{e}^{t/2},3⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨0,1⟩$ when $t=2,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=0.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨1-{e}^{t/2},3⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (1-{e}^{t/2})\,\text{d}t,\int 3\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t-2{e}^{t/2}+{C}_{1},3t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(2)=⟨0,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨2-2{e}^{2/2}+{C}_{1},3(2)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,1⟩ & =⟨2-2e+{C}_{1},6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=2e-2$ and ${C}_{2}=-5.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨t-2{e}^{t/2}+2e-2,3t-5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨0-2{e}^{0/2}+2e-2,3(0)-5⟩ \\  & =⟨2e-4,-5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

a
t=4
b
No stationary points
c
t=1,2
d
t=2

t=2,4
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating and using v(3)=⟨−1,1⟩ gives v(t)=⟨t²−6t+8,|t−2|^(4/3)⟩. The first component vanishes at t=2 and t=4; the second vanishes only at t=2. Both are zero only at t=2.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨2t-6,\frac{4}{3}\sqrt[3]{t-2}⟩,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨-1,1⟩$ when $t=3,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-6,\frac{4}{3}\sqrt[3]{t-2}⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t,\int \frac{4}{3}\sqrt[3]{t-2}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{1},\sqrt[3]{(t-2)^{4}}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(3)=⟨-1,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨{3}^{2}-6(3)+{C}_{1},\sqrt[3]{(3-2)^{4}}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,1⟩ & =⟨-9+{C}_{1},1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=8$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨{t}^{2}-6t+8,\sqrt[3]{(t-2)^{4}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨{t}^{2}-6t+8,\sqrt[3]{(t-2)^{4}}⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-6t+8=(t-2)(t-4) & =0\,⇒\,t=2,4, \\ \sqrt[3]{(t-2)^{4}} & =0\,⇒\,t=2.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=2,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

a
t=4
b
No stationary points
c
t=1,2
d
t=2
e
t=2,4
Submit

EXPLANATION

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨2t−6,43t−23⟩dt=⟨∫(2t−6)dt,∫43t−23dt⟩=⟨t2−6t+C1,(t−2)43+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(3)=⟨−1,1⟩. Substituting t=3, we get

v(3)=⟨32−6(3)+C1,(3−2)43+C2⟩⟨−1,1⟩=⟨−9+C1,1+C2⟩, so we must have C1=8 and C2=0. Therefore, the velocity is given by v(t)=⟨t2−6t+8,(t−2)43⟩.

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero: v(t)=0⟨t2−6t+8,(t−2)43⟩=⟨0,0⟩

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Points at Which a Particle is Stationary Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨2t-6,\frac{4}{3}\sqrt[3]{t-2}⟩,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨-1,1⟩$ when $t=3,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
content.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-6,\frac{4}{3}\sqrt[3]{t-2}⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t,\int \frac{4}{3}\sqrt[3]{t-2}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{1},\sqrt[3]{(t-2)^{4}}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(3)=⟨-1,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨{3}^{2}-6(3)+{C}_{1},\sqrt[3]{(3-2)^{4}}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,1⟩ & =⟨-9+{C}_{1},1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=8$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨{t}^{2}-6t+8,\sqrt[3]{(t-2)^{4}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨{t}^{2}-6t+8,\sqrt[3]{(t-2)^{4}}⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-6t+8=(t-2)(t-4) & =0\,⇒\,t=2,4, \\ \sqrt[3]{(t-2)^{4}} & =0\,⇒\,t=2.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=2,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨-1,2⟩,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨-1,2⟩$ when $t=2,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨-1,2⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (-1)\,\text{d}t,\int 2\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-t+{C}_{1},2t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(2)=⟨-1,2⟩.$ Substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨-2+{C}_{1},2(2)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,2⟩ & =⟨-2+{C}_{1},4+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=1$ and ${C}_{2}=-2.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨1-t,2t-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1-t,2t-2⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}1-t & =0\,⇒\,t=1, \\ 2t-2=2(t-1) & =0\,⇒\,t=1.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=1,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩,\,0\le t<\pi .
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨1,1⟩$ when $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t,\int 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(\frac{\pi }{4})=⟨1,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=1$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need

$$
\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1 & =0\,⇒\,t=0, \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\,⇒\,t=0,\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=0,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨2sin⁡(2t),2cos⁡(2t)⟩dt=⟨∫2sin⁡(2t)dt,∫2cos⁡(2t)dt⟩=⟨−cos⁡(2t)+C1,sin⁡(2t)+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(π4)=⟨1,1⟩. Substituting t=π4, we get

v(π4)=⟨−cos⁡(2⋅π4)+C1,sin⁡(2⋅π4)+C2⟩⟨1,1⟩=⟨C1,1+C2⟩,

so we must have C1=1 and C2=0. Therefore, the velocity is given by

v(t)=⟨−cos⁡(2t)+1,sin⁡(2t)⟩.

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

v(t)=0⟨−cos⁡(2t)+1,sin⁡(2t)⟩=⟨0,0⟩

So, we need −cos⁡(2t)+1=0⇒t=0,sin⁡(2t)=0⇒t=0,π2.

The only solution that satisfies both equations is t=0, so this is the only value of t when the particle is stationary.

$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨-1,\,-14⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨{1}^{1/2}+{C}_{1},\,2\cdot {1}^{3/2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,\,-14⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},\,2+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨{t}^{1/2}-2,\,2{t}^{3/2}-16⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨{t}^{1/2}-2,\,2{t}^{3/2}-16⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},3\sqrt{t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 3\sqrt{t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{1/2}+{C}_{1},\,2{t}^{3/2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨-1,\,-14⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨{1}^{1/2}+{C}_{1},\,2\cdot {1}^{3/2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,\,-14⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},\,2+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have ${C}_{1}=-2$ and ${C}_{2}=-16.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨{t}^{1/2}-2,\,2{t}^{3/2}-16⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨{t}^{1/2}-2,\,2{t}^{3/2}-16⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{1/2}-2=0 & \,⇒\,{t}^{1/2}=2\,⇒\,t=4, \\ 2{t}^{3/2}-16=0 & \,⇒\,{t}^{3/2}=8\,⇒\,t=4.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=4.$ So, this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.
